source_text:
Ἔδειξέ μοι δένδρα πολλὰ μὴ ἔχοντα φύλλα, ἀλλ’ ὡσεὶ ξηρὰ ἐδόκει μοι εἶναι: ὅμοια γὰρ ἧν πάντα. καὶ λέγει μοι: Βλέπεις τὰ δένδρα ταῦτα; Βλέπω, φημί, κύριε, ὅμοια ὄντα καὶ ξηρά. ἀπο κριθείς μοι λέγει: Ταῦτα τὰ δένδρα, ἃ βλέπεις, οἱ κατοικοῦντές εἰσιν ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ.
Διατί οὖν, φημί, κύριε, ὡσεὶ ξηρά εἰσι καὶ ὅμοια; Ὅτι, φησίν, οὔτε οἱ δίκαιοι φαίνονται οὔτε οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλ’ ὅμοιοί εἰσιν: ὁ γὰρ αἰὼν οὗτος τοῖς δικαίοις χειμών ἐστι, καὶ οὐ φαίνονται μετὰ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν κατοικοῦντες.
ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ χειμῶνι τὰ δένδρα ἀποβεβληκότα τὰ φύλλα ὅμοιά εἰσι καὶ οὐ φαίνονται τὰ ξηρὰ ποῖά εἰσιν ἢ τὰ ζῶντα, οὕτως ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ οὐ φαίνονται οὔτε οἱ δίκαιοι οὔτε οἱ ἁμαρτωλοί, ἀλλὰ πάντες ὅμοιοί εἰσιν.
thought_title: The winter of this age hides righteous and sinners alike
orientation: The Shepherd shows Hermas a stand of leafless trees. They picture how the righteous and the sinners cannot be told apart in this present age.
pass_a_gloss: He showed me many trees not having leaves, but as if dry they seemed to me to be; for alike were all. And he says to me: Do you see these trees? I see, I say, lord, alike being and dry. Answering me he says: These trees, which you see, are those dwelling in this age. Why then, I say, lord, as if dry are they and alike? Because, he says, neither the righteous appear nor the sinners in this age, but alike they are; for this age for the righteous winter is, and they do not appear dwelling with the sinners. For just as in winter the trees having cast off the leaves alike are and it is not apparent which are the dry ones or the living ones, so in this age neither the righteous appear nor the sinners, but all alike are.

choices.english: as if dry they seemed to me to be
choices.why: Keeps the impressionistic force of 'as if' and the dative of the perceiver, preserving the visionary's subjective perception rather than stating a fact

choices.term: οἱ κατοικοῦντές εἰσιν ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ
choices.english: are those dwelling in this age
choices.why: The present participle 'dwelling' preserves the ongoing state of inhabiting this present age, matching the Shepherd's explanatory identification
rejected: are the inhabitants of this age
are those who live in this age

choices.term: ὁ γὰρ αἰὼν οὗτος τοῖς δικαίοις χειμών ἐστι
choices.english: for this age for the righteous winter is
choices.why: The word order places 'winter' as the predicate climax, and the dative 'for the righteous' marks those affected; keeping this order preserves the aphoristic force
rejected: for this age is winter to the righteous
for this age is a winter for the righteous

choices.why: The perfect participle conveys a completed action with ongoing result, matching the Greek's depiction of trees in their leafless winter state

choices.english: which are the dry ones or the living ones
choices.why: The interrogative 'which' preserves the question of identification embedded in the comparison, and the substantivized adjectives keep the contrast between dry and living trees
rejected: which are dry and which are alive
what kind are dry or living

pass_b_english: The Shepherd showed me many trees that had no leaves. They seemed to me to be dry, for they were all alike. He said to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see them, sir,” I said. “They are all alike, and dry.” He answered me, “These trees that you see are the people who live in this age.”

“Then why, sir,” I asked, “do they seem dry, and all alike?” “Because,” he said, “in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are plain to see. They are alike. For this age is winter for the righteous, and they are not plain to see, because they live among the sinners.

“In winter the trees have shed their leaves and are all alike, and it is not plain to see which are dry and which are living. In the same way, in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are plain to see. All are alike.”
